Hi Alex —

Thanks again for the call this morning — really helpful to understand FinApps' architecture and primary integration goals. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can land the architecture workshop: 

Call summary:
- Attendees: Alex (FinApps), Marissa (Redwood SE), Rishi (Redwood Solutions Architect), David (Redwood PM)
- Primary use cases: structured document processing + enriched search (embeddings + reranker) and a small number of external actions (payments, account updates) behind your internal services.
- Key non-functional constraints: 99th p latency budget of 400ms for interactive flows, customer-managed KMS requirement for PII, and multi-region routing for US/EU customers.

Integration / architecture topics to cover (first pass):
1) SDK setup: Redwood provides JS and Python SDKs. For production we recommend the server-side SDK in a VPC-peered environment or your backend service calling the Redwood Private endpoint.
2) Auth: two supported patterns — API keys for hosted, or mTLS + KMS-backed tokens for Private deployments. We can support your CMK via our KMS integration.
3) Routing & model selection: route by region + profile (latency vs cost). We can pin the reranker/embedding model pair for consistent scoring.
4) Structured output & tool/function calling:
   - Define each tool with a clear schema (input fields, allowed types, success/failure responses).
   - Use explicit schemas for structured output so outputs can be validated and surfaced directly in your workflow.
   - For sensitive actions (payments, user updates) we recommend an approval step server-side (Redwood returns structured intent + args; your service verifies before action).
5) Embeddings & reranker:
   - Use sentence-transformer style vectors for retrieval; surface top-K candidates, then run a small reranker (cross-encoder) for final ordering.
   - Cache vectors and use TTL-based invalidation for cost control.
6) Tool/function calling integration patterns (high level):
   - Tool definitions: central registry of tools with versioned schemas; SDK supports sending tool metadata alongside prompts.
   - Tool choice: prefer domain-specific tools for deterministic ops (payments) and model-invoked lookup tools for fuzzy retrieval.
   - Parallel tools: fan-out from a coordinator to call multiple tools in parallel, then aggregate results back to the model as structured inputs.
   - Error handling: per-tool retries with exponential backoff, circuit-breaker for noisy services, and an async DLQ for long-running failures.

Attachments: architecture-diagram.pdf (attached) — high-level flow we sketched.

Proposed next steps:
- Schedule a 90-min architecture workshop with your backend + security (can we do next Wed 3/24 or Thu 3/25?)
- I’ll circulate an initial design doc + sample tool definitions ahead of the workshop.
- Please share a list of the external actions (endpoints + auth types) you want the model to trigger as pre-work.

Thanks — looking forward to the workshop.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Alex —

Great questions — answers inline below + a sample tool-definitions JSON attached.

1) Example repo / SDK patterns:
- We have a JS example showing the Redwood SDK used server-side to register tool metadata and perform function-calling. Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/examples/tree/main/tool-calling-js (see README + /examples/payment_flow.js)
- Key patterns: register tool schema at startup, validate model arguments server-side, and use the SDK's streaming to return structured tool outputs to the client.

2) Parallel tools coordination:
- Two common options: (A) Orchestrator-first: your coordinator service fans out parallel tool calls, aggregates results, and sends a single combined context back to the model (best for strict latency budgets). (B) Model-first with async updates: model requests tools, you return partials as they arrive via streaming or a follow-up message; needs careful idempotency and correlation IDs.
- Recommendation: start with orchestrator-first for deterministic latency — coordinator issues parallel calls with a short per-tool timeout (e.g., 250ms), then sends aggregated results. If a tool times out, mark it as partial and optionally fetch full result async.

3) CMK and Private deployment:
- Yes — Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS keys (AWS KMS + GCP CMEK). We can enable your CMK during deployment; will require a short security review and an IAM trust policy.
- I’ll attach our security brief (SOC2 + customer-managed KMS section) for your infosec.

4) Sample tool definition (attached tool-definitions-sample.json) — highlights:
- name: canonical tool id
- version: semver
- input_schema: JSON Schema for input args
- output_schema: JSON Schema for structured response
- timeout_ms: execution timeout default
- retry_policy: {"strategy":"exponential_backoff","max_retries":2} 

5) Error handling patterns:
- Per-tool retries with backoff (do not retry idempotent state-changing ops without an idempotency key).
- Circuit breaker: open after X failures to prevent cascading latency.
- DLQ / async reconciliation: for non-blocking ops, hand off failures to an async workflow and surface a user-friendly result to the model.

Next steps I’ll take this week:
- Share the example repo and attached sample tool-definitions JSON (attached)
- Book the 90-min architecture workshop for Thu 2026-03-25 11:00am PT — calendar invite to follow.

Pre-work for your team: please send a list of endpoints (path + auth type) and the intended action for each (read-only vs state-change) so we can map required schemas.

Best,
Marissa
